Die without a will?
The state decides

lines.text: In 2025, only 24% of surveyed Americans had a will.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, only twenty-four percent of surveyed Americans had a will.

lines.text: Without one, state law has a default plan.
lines.say: Without one, state law has a default plan.

lines.text: That 24% is down from 33% in 2022, per Caring.com's yearly surveys.
lines.say: That twenty-four percent is down from thirty-three percent in twenty twenty-two, according to Caring dot com's yearly surveys.

lines.text: The rules vary by state. In New York, a spouse with kids gets the first $50,000 plus half the rest.
lines.say: The rules vary by state. In New York, a spouse with kids gets the first fifty thousand dollars, plus half of the rest.

lines.text: Example: on a $250,000 estate, the spouse gets $150,000 and the kids share $100,000.
lines.say: So on a two hundred fifty thousand dollar estate, the spouse gets one hundred fifty thousand dollars, and the kids share one hundred thousand.

lines.text: An unmarried partner, even after 20 years? Under New York's intestacy law, $0.
lines.say: And an unmarried partner, even after twenty years together? Under New York's intestacy law, zero dollars.

lines.text: No relatives at all? Under the Uniform Probate Code, a model many states use, the estate goes to the state.

post.title: Only 24% had a will in 2025. Here's the default plan
post.ig:
Only 24% of surveyed Americans had a will in 2025. Without one, state law has a default plan.

Dying without a will is called intestacy, and the rules vary by state.
In New York, a spouse with kids gets the first $50,000 plus half the rest. On a $250,000 estate (hypothetical), that's $150,000 to the spouse and $100,000 to the kids.
Unmarried partners get $0 under New York's intestacy law. Under the Uniform Probate Code, with no relatives, the estate goes to the state.

Sources: Caring.com Wills and Estate Planning Study (2022-2025); NY EPTL 4-1.1; Uniform Probate Code 2-102, 2-105.
